extracted.intended_audience: model aeroplane builders, experimenters, and amateur aeronautical designers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical design and construction guidance for small model aeroplanes, with emphasis on automatic stability, arrangement of surfaces, and rubber-motor (elastic) propulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic stability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any model flying machine (in the absence of a pilot) must possess a high degree of automatic stability. The model must be so constructed as to be naturally stable, in the medium through which it is proposed to drive it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is essential for successful flight; stability must be considered both theoretically and practically. Emphasis that stability must be inherent to the model, not reliant on active piloting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concave-under surfaces unstable without balancing device
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces concave on the under side are not stable unless some form of balancing device (such as a tail, etc.) is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers using concave-under aerofoils must provide separate balancing surfaces (tail, elevator) to achieve stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium tendency for stability
rubrics_metrics.description: If an aeroplane is in equilibrium and moving uniformly, it is necessary for stability that it shall tend towards a condition of equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability requires that perturbations produce restoring tendencies back to equilibrium rather than divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillation damping
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of 'oscillations' it is absolutely necessary for stability that these oscillations shall decrease in amplitude, in other words, be damped out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (geometry, control surfaces, damping mechanisms) should ensure oscillations are self-damping rather than growing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger from excessive dihedral or very low centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: In aeroplanes in which the dihedral angle is excessive or the centre of gravity very low down, a dangerous pitching motion is quite likely to be set up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to ship metacentre: too much 'static' stability can induce dynamic instability; avoid extreme dihedral or excessively low CG.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller shaft through centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The propeller shaft should pass through the centre of gravity of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If propulsive action does not pass through CG the system becomes 'acentric' producing upsetting couples; alignment is critical for balance and to avoid upsetting moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front planes angle greater than rear ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The front planes should be at a greater angle of inclination than the rear ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of longitudinal stability arrangement — helps set up restoring moments between main aerofoil and balancer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal stability reduces when climbing
rubrics_metrics.description: The longitudinal stability of an aeroplane grows much less when the aeroplane commences to rise, a monoplane becoming unstable when the angle of ascent is greater than the inclination of the main aerofoil to the horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for worst-case climb angles; be aware stable trim in level flight may not hold in ascent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head resistance increases stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Head resistance increases stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing some head resistance (drag at the nose/forward surfaces) can have a stabilising effect; consider where drag is acceptable to improve inherent stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three planes more stable than two
rubrics_metrics.description: Three planes are more stable than two. [Elevator--main aerofoil--horizontal rudder behind.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A three-plane configuration (elevator, main aerofoil, tail) generally increases longitudinal stability; many full-sized designs use this to good effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gliding more stable than horizontal flight
rubrics_metrics.description: When an aeroplane is gliding (downwards) stability is greater than in horizontal flight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect different stability characteristics in glide vs powered/level flight; plan balancing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large moment of inertia hurts stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A large moment of inertia is inimical (opposed) to stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessarily high rotational inertia (mass far from CG) which slows damping and can promote oscillations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible loss of stability at high speeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Aeroplanes (naturally) stable up to a certain velocity (speed) may become unstable when moving beyond that speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential causes: turbulence over aerofoil edges changing streamlines, structural deformation. Test high-speed behavior; do not assume static stability holds at higher speeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced glider needs negative-angle separate surface
rubrics_metrics.description: In a balanced glider for stability a separate surface at a negative angle to the line of flight is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare with front/rear surface arrangements; ensure a balancing surface with appropriate negative incidence is provided for stable gliding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keel (vertical fin) placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A keel surface should be situated well above and behind the centre of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to instinct to place fin below CG, practical experiments show placing fin above and behind CG can increase stability; test vertical fin placement relative to CG.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aeroplane is conservative system: stability vs kinetic energy
rubrics_metrics.description: An aeroplane is a conservative system, and stability is greatest when the kinetic energy is a maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration with pendulum: high kinetic energy states can correspond to greater dynamic stability; consider energy states when assessing stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidence of centres and propulsive action alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: THE CENTRES OF GRAVITY, OF PRESSURE, OF HEAD RESISTANCE, SHOULD BE COINCIDENT, AND THE PROPULSIVE ACTION OF THE PROPELLER PASS THROUGH THIS SAME POINT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary mechanics: if these centres do not coincide an 'acentric' couple will arise upsetting the machine. Aim to align CG, centre of pressure, centre of head resistance, and propulsive thrust line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal surface separation (four-times rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: For automatic longitudinal stability the two surfaces, the aerofoil proper and the balancer (elevator or tail, or both), must be separated by some considerable distance, a distance not less than four times the width of the main aerofoil. More is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation is critical — early experimenters failed because main aerofoil and balancer were contiguous; practical examples (Pénaud, Farman vs Wright) show long moment arms improve automatic stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended incidence settings for three-surface models
rubrics_metrics.description: With three surfaces one would set the elevator at a slight plus angle, main aerofoil horizontal (neither positive nor negative), and the tail at a corresponding negative angle to the positive one of the elevator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement helps to balance lift/trimming and counteracts centre of pressure travel; small adjustments fine-tune longitudinal trim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making dihedral angle excessive
rubrics_metrics.description: It is quite a mistake to make the (dihedral) angle excessive, the 'lift' being thereby diminished. A few degrees should suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dihedral promotes transverse stability but too much reduces overall lift; aim for modest dihedral (a few degrees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Upturned tip (dihedral) recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: The outer edges of the aerofoil then should be turned upward for the purpose of transverse stability, while the inner surface should remain flat or concave for greater support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'upturned tip' dihedral seems advantageous: upturned outer edges for righting moment, inner area flat/concave for lift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Righting moment larger at outer edge
rubrics_metrics.description: It is evident that the righting moment of a unit of surface of an aeroplane is greater at the outer edge than elsewhere, owing to the greater lever arm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cross-sections and spanwise lift distribution recognizing outer panels produce larger restoring moments; favors wingtip dihedral or design choices leveraging lever arm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of long moment arms and long rubber strands
rubrics_metrics.description: Pénaud ... also the necessity for using long strands of rubber. Some of his models flew 150 ft., and showed considerable stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long rubber strands allow more turns and smoother torque; correlates with the general principle: long moment-arm separation improves stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber motors preferred for small/light models
rubrics_metrics.description: For the smaller and lighter class of models there is no likelihood of rubber being displaced; no better substitute has been found for elastic (rubber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubber provides highest energy per weight for small models; prefer rubber for lightweight model propulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber extension behavior: proportionalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension is (initially) proportional to the weight suspended, but soon an increasing increase of extension; extension is inversely proportional to the thickness; in a rubber cord the extension is directly proportional to the length as well as inversely proportional to the thickness and to the weight suspended—true only within the limits of elasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design elastic motors accounting for non-linear stretch behavior, time-dependent creep (permanent set), and size-thickness-length relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid permanent loading of rubber cords
rubrics_metrics.description: An elastic cord or spring balance should never have a weight left permanently on it—or be subjected to a distorting force for a long time than necessary, or it will take a 'permanent set,' and not return to even approximately its original length or form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not store rubber under tension; remove loads and avoid prolonged strain to preserve elasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber volume increases on stretching
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Rubber Cord is stretched there is an Increase of Volume. On stretching a piece of rubber cord to twice its original natural length ... it is about two-thirds of its former volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect cross-sectional change not simply inverse proportional to length; affects packing and coil behaviour in motors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber motors: torque vs number/length of strands
rubrics_metrics.description: A. Increasing the number of (rubber) strands by one-half (length and thickness remaining constant) increases the torque twofold. B. Doubling the number of strands increases the torque more than three times—about 3-1/3 times... C. Trebling the number of strands increases the torque at least seven times. D. Doubling the number of strands (length, etc., remaining constant) diminishes the number of turns by one-third to one-half. E. If we halve the length of rubber strands keeping the number same torque slightly increased for first 100 turns but at 240 turns it is double. F. No arrangement of strands per se gets more energy than any other, but there are reasons for making strands long and few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use long, relatively few strands to maximize usable turns and smooth torque; expect non-linear scaling of torque with strand count and tradeoffs with number of turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule of rubber strand length
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the rubber strands twice in feet the number of the strands in inches, e.g., if the number of strands is 12 their length should be 2 ft., if 18, 3 ft., and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this heuristic to choose strand length relative to strand count for smooth torque and good performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ball bearings to obviate end thrust
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirty-six strands ... at 150 turns give a torque of 4 oz. on a 5-in. arm, but an end thrust, or end pull, of about 3½ lb. (Ball bearings, or some such device, can be used to obviate this end thrust when desirable.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design motor mounts and bearing arrangements to handle axial loads; ball bearings are recommended to reduce friction and handle end thrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisted rubber coils: maximum turns and life
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubber motor in which the double knot is not exceeded by more than 100 turns (rubber one yard in length) should last a good time. When trying for a record flight ... as many as even 500 or 600 or even more turns have been given ... but such a severe strain soon spoils the rubber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extreme overwinding if longevity is required; use moderate turns for lasting motors, extreme turns may be for one-off records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lubricants: avoid oils, recommend glycerine or soda/chalk
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything of an oily or greasy nature has an injurious effect on the rubber... The only oil which is said to have no action on rubber ... is castor oil; all the same, I do not advise its use. There are three only which we need consider: 1. Soda and water. 2. French chalk. 3. Pure redistilled glycerine. The third, glycerine, is for ordinary purposes by far the best, and has a beneficial rather than a deleterious effect on the rubber; but it must be pure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pure redistilled glycerine sparingly to lubricate strands (prevents sticking and increases number turns). Avoid petroleum products, benzol, turpentine, vaseline, etc. Wash periodically in warm soda to remove dirt before re-glycerining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep rubber strands separated and clean
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the chief causes of this (rubber deterioration) is that the strands stick together—they should always be carefully separated, if necessary, after a flight—and an undue strain is thereby cast on certain parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After flights, separate coils, clean off grit/dust, apply glycerine prudently; prevents unequal tension and premature failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copper and rubber incompatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Action of Copper upon Rubber: Copper, whether in the form of the metal, the oxides, or the soluble salts, has a marked injurious action upon rubber. In no case should the strands be placed upon bare metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contact between rubber and copper parts; cover hooks/attachments with valve tubing or equivalent insulating material to prevent chemical/oxidative damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve rubber: storage and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve rubber it should be kept from the sun's rays, or, indeed, any actinic rays, in a cool, airy place, and subjected to as even a temperature as possible. Great extremes of temperature have a very injurious effect on rubber, and it should be washed from time to time in warm soda water. It should be subjected to no tension or compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buy fresh Para rubber, store cool/dry/shaded, avoid prolonged tension, wash and recondition as necessary; vulcanized rubber contains ~3% sulphur making it prone to oxidation so freshness matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test criteria for good rubber
rubrics_metrics.description: Good elastic thread composed of pure Para rubber and sulphur should, if properly made, stretch to seven times its length, and then return to its original length. It should also possess a stretching limit at least ten times its original length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect strands microscopically for clean cut edges (less ragged); prefer well-cut strands to maximize life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section shape and size for rubber strands
rubrics_metrics.description: The square and not the ribbon or strip should be used. ... Theoretically no doubt a round section would be best, but none such (in small sizes) is on the market. ... One-sixteenth or one-twelfth is the best size for ordinary models; personally, I prefer the thinner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use square-section strands of approximately 1/16 or 1/12 inch for ordinary models; avoid tubular sections and ribbon strips (more ragged edges and less efficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geared rubber motors generally disadvantageous
rubrics_metrics.description: It is quite a mistake to suppose that any advantage can be obtained by using a four to one gearing, say; all that you do obtain is one-fourth of the power minus the increased friction, minus the added weight. This presumes, of course, you make no alteration in your rubber strands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heavy gearing ratios which shorten strand length, increase friction and weight; splitting rubber into multiple sets may give more turns but requires more strands to maintain thrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: If using geared twin-equal-wheels, minimize weight/friction and maximise strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The only geared arrangement worth consideration is one in which two gear wheels—same size, weight, and number of teeth—are made use of, the propeller being attached to the axle of one of them, and the same number of strands are used on each axle. The friction and weight must be reduced to a minimum, and the strength be a maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use steel accurately cut cogwheels, solid but lightened by drilling, light ball bearings, minimum framework weight (thin tinned sheet-iron), steel pianoforte wire spindles and hooks. Use vaseline on cogs to make them run easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin screws and splitting rubber
rubrics_metrics.description: Supposing we have a model with one propeller and 36 strands of elastic. If we decide to fit it with twin screws ... we shall require two sets of strands of more than 18 in number each to have the same motive power (27 if the same torque be required). Do not attempt to split up the rubber into more than two strands to each propeller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan strand count when using multiple propellers; splitting reduces available torque per propeller unless strand count increased; avoid excessive splitting which reduces effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of allowable turns related to strand count (knot/test data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of turns to produce a double knot in the cord (one yard long): 4 strands -> 440 turns; 8 -> 310; 12 -> 250; 16 -> 200; 28 -> 170. The greater the number of strands used in a given length, the fewer turns will it stand in proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these empirical numbers to estimate maximum safe winding before failure (double-knot), noting longer strands and fewer strands allow more turns. Factor into motor design and charging procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber rupture stress & permissible stress
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubber has rupture stress of 330 lb. per sq. in., but a very high permissible stress, as much as 80 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand material limits: although strong, extreme strains shorten life; plan operating stresses conservatively below rupture/permissible limits for durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber vs steel springs energy density
rubrics_metrics.description: One pound weight of elastic can be made to store up some 320 ft.-lb. of energy, and steel only some 65 lb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubber stores far more energy per weight than steel springs for model motors—prefer rubber for energy-dense, lightweight motors unless other considerations dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressed-air motors practical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Compressed air motors appear ideal on paper but are limited by reservoir weight, achievable pressure, and volume; example: small reservoir gives only 10 to 30 seconds flight at 80 lb. pressure and the receiver weight may be significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider realistic reservoir mass, filling effort (many pump strokes), and short run times; compressed-air motors may not be practical for sustained model flights compared to rubber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using oils/solvents that dissolve or harm rubber
rubrics_metrics.description: Ether, chloroform, carbon-tetrachloride, turpentine, carbon bi-sulphide, petroleum spirit, benzene ... dissolve rubber readily. Alcohol is absorbed but not a solvent. Anything oily or greasy must be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep rubber away from solvents and petroleum products; clean and maintain with recommended agents only.
